On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. source.text:
On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. But the samples Cordelia carried home in her rucksack made her famous, the crystal cave was named after the village of Sennick, and the climbers always insisted that the real hero of the journey had been a goat called Mabel.

parts.before: In the winter of 721, the Chandlers' Guild petitioned the council for the right to hold a market in the Narrows.
parts.text: The shipwrights bought 56 barrels of pitch brought from the forest of Blackwold.
parts.after: A dispute over a stolen weathervane between two families of the Narrows occupied the magistrates for 2 weeks.

parts.before: Pilgrims came to the Chapel of the Tides in great numbers, many of them from the hill villages around Marrowby.
parts.text: Charcoal-burners from the forest of Blackwold delivered 68 more barrels of pitch before the rains.
parts.after: The Jarnwell family of Highmarket sent their youngest son to be apprenticed to a glassblower in Saltings.

parts.before: Around this time, the council met 31 times that year, mostly to argue about the drains of Saltings.
parts.text: A last load of 19 barrels of pitch came from the forest of Blackwold in the autumn.
parts.after: Ships from Carrowmouth crowded the harbour; the Restless Gull alone carried 42 bales of wine.

decoys.before: The year 704 opened with rumours of war beyond the mountains.
decoys.text: The forest of Blackwood supplied 79 barrels of pitch, but the shipwrights judged it poor.
decoys.after: Perrin Carrgrave and Anselm Corford were seen arguing on Sparrow Yard about the price of timber, to the delight of the passers-by.

parts.before: The market in Rookhill moved from Sparrow Yard to the square in front of the Temple of the Lamp.
parts.text: The census of 743 counted 5,372 households within the walls.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, many of the older houses on Brine Way were rebuilt in brick after the long storm.

parts.before: According to the guild rolls, many of the older houses on Rope Walk were rebuilt in brick after the great fire.
parts.text: Clerks later found an error in the census of 743: the true count was 6,202 households within the walls.

parts.before: The city walls were patched along 148 yards of their length near the Drovers' Gate.
parts.text: The founders' chest buried beneath the Founders' Arch was opened before the whole council and found to hold 879 silver coins.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, Leopold Jarnwell, a bookbinder from Highmarket, was remembered long afterwards for writing a satirical song about the council.

decoys.before: A travelling company of players performed on Flint Way, and one of their comedies was promptly banned by the aldermen.
decoys.text: A second chest, dug up under the Old Weighhouse, held 897 copper coins and a broken key.

parts.before: It is also recorded that the Tide Festival was kept with unusual splendour, and 274 paper lanterns were floated down the river.
parts.text: The races at the Apple Wake were won that year by a grey mare called Duchess of Mists.
parts.after: The price of dyed cloth rose to 11 silver marks a sack, and the people of Mudwharf grumbled about it in every tavern.

decoys.before: A scholar named Wenna Iverwell began a catalogue of the city's books, which was still unfinished forty years later.
decoys.text: A chestnut colt named Quicksilver Jenny came second in the races at the Apple Wake, to the fury of his owner.
decoys.after: Yannick Dunnwick left a bequest of 380 gold crowns to the almshouse on Copper Row.

parts.before: Wilmot Halley was appointed keeper of the city granary and held the post for 17 years.
parts.text: That year the watchword of the Night Watch was "quicksilver", and anyone abroad after curfew had to give it.
parts.after: Merchants from the Amber Coast brought news of war in the south, and prices rose accordingly.

decoys.before: Wolves were seen on the hills above Marrowby, and the shepherds kept watch in pairs.
decoys.text: The Day Watch, never to be outdone, chose the word "juniper".
decoys.after: Meanwhile, the market in Rookhill moved from Brine Way to the square in front of St. Bertram's.

parts.before: A fire broke out in a bookbinder's workshop on Anchor Way, but it was put out before it could spread to the Glass Steps.
parts.text: In those years the Tanners' Guild was led by Lisbet Sorrwick.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, Jorund Veyford, a lamplighter from Rookhill, was remembered long afterwards for writing a satirical song about the council.

parts.text: Lisbet Sorrwick died of a fever in the year 776 and was buried at St. Wendreda's.
parts.after: The chronicler notes, with some disapproval, that the Tanners' Guild spent 466 copper pennies on a single banquet that year.

decoys.before: The council met 7 times that year, mostly to argue about the drains of the Tanners' Quarter.
decoys.text: Lisbet Zorrwick, a wealthy wine merchant, died in the year 784.

parts.before: The harvest in the valley was poor, and bread was rationed in Lowbridge until the spring.
parts.text: The famous Widow's Stew of Fishergate called for exactly 15 threads of saffron, no more and no fewer.
parts.after: The toll-keepers of the Old Bridge went on strike, and for a week nobody could cross without paying twice.

decoys.before: It is also recorded that the Fishwives' Guild quarrelled with the Glassblowers' Guild over the use of the old weighhouse, and the matter went before the magistrates.
decoys.text: Salt-Crust Bream, its humbler cousin, used 35 cloves instead.
decoys.after: Meanwhile, a scholar named Wilmot Halley began a catalogue of the city's books, which was still unfinished forty years later.

parts.before: A fire broke out in a stonemason's workshop on Tallow Way, but it was put out before it could spread to the Old Harbour.
parts.text: On her last voyage the Crooked Pilgrim was commanded by Captain Soren Corby.
parts.after: It was, by all accounts, a quiet summer in Saltings.

parts.before: Later that year, a travelling company of players performed on Tallow Way, and one of their comedies was promptly banned by the aldermen.
parts.text: Soren Corby had been born in the hill village of Fernhollow, far from any sea.
parts.after: Rain fell for 4 days without stopping, and the lower streets of the Tanners' Quarter stood knee-deep in water.

decoys.before: Elowen Haldal and Greta Narkdal were seen arguing on Rope Walk about the price of herring, to the delight of the passers-by.
decoys.text: Captain Soren Korby was born in Wrenfold and never once lost a ship.
decoys.after: Nothing of great note happened in the Old Harbour that summer, except that a bear escaped from the menagerie and was found asleep in the Temple of the Lamp.

parts.before: The market in the Upper Terraces moved from Tallow Way to the square in front of the Temple of the Lamp.
parts.text: The Lightning Oak in the Old Green, the oldest tree in the city, was measured at 37 feet around the trunk.
parts.after: Pilgrims came to St. Ilse's in great numbers, many of them from the hill villages around Pellow Cross.

decoys.text: The Crooked Elm, which stood not far away, measured 33 feet around.
decoys.after: Cressen Garmore left a bequest of 367 copper pennies to the almshouse on Rope Walk.

parts.before: The coopers of Rookhill complained that the new regulations of the Apothecaries' Guild were written only to ruin them.
parts.text: The treaty of friendship with Karane was signed on the 12th day of April, in the hall of the Ropemakers' Guild.
parts.after: Rain fell for 22 days without stopping, and the lower streets of the Tanners' Quarter stood knee-deep in water.

decoys.before: The toll-keepers of the Cooper's Bridge went on strike, and for a week nobody could cross without paying twice.
decoys.text: A trade agreement with Caelholm followed on the 14th day of April.
decoys.after: The Carrdal family of Mudwharf sent their youngest son to be apprenticed to a bargemaster in the Old Harbour.

source.text:
On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. But the samples Cordelia carried home in her rucksack made her famous, the crystal cave was named after the village of Sennick, and the climbers always insisted that the real hero of the journey had been a goat called Mabel.

source.text:
On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

Their base camp stood beside a frozen lake that the villagers called the Black Tarn. The expedition's doctor, Benedek Krauss, carried a medicine chest and a fiddle, which he played badly every night. The oldest climber was Brenna Brodsky, who was 59 years old and had climbed with the leader's father. The supplies had been carried up from the valley by 16 mules.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. But the samples Cordelia carried home in her rucksack made her famous, the crystal cave was named after the village of Sennick, and the climbers always insisted that the real hero of the journey had been a goat called Mabel.

parts.before: In the winter of 721, the Chandlers' Guild petitioned the council for the right to hold a market in the Narrows.
parts.text: The shipwrights bought 56 barrels of pitch brought from the forest of Blackwold.
parts.after: A dispute over a stolen weathervane between two families of the Narrows occupied the magistrates for 2 weeks.

parts.before: Pilgrims came to the Chapel of the Tides in great numbers, many of them from the hill villages around Marrowby.
parts.text: Charcoal-burners from the forest of Blackwold delivered 68 more barrels of pitch before the rains.
parts.after: The Jarnwell family of Highmarket sent their youngest son to be apprenticed to a glassblower in Saltings.

parts.before: Around this time, the council met 31 times that year, mostly to argue about the drains of Saltings.
parts.text: A last load of 19 barrels of pitch came from the forest of Blackwold in the autumn.
parts.after: Ships from Carrowmouth crowded the harbour; the Restless Gull alone carried 42 bales of wine.

decoys.before: The year 704 opened with rumours of war beyond the mountains.
decoys.text: The forest of Blackwood supplied 79 barrels of pitch, but the shipwrights judged it poor.
decoys.after: Perrin Carrgrave and Anselm Corford were seen arguing on Sparrow Yard about the price of timber, to the delight of the passers-by.

parts.before: The market in Rookhill moved from Sparrow Yard to the square in front of the Temple of the Lamp.
parts.text: The census of 743 counted 5,372 households within the walls.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, many of the older houses on Brine Way were rebuilt in brick after the long storm.

parts.before: According to the guild rolls, many of the older houses on Rope Walk were rebuilt in brick after the great fire.
parts.text: Clerks later found an error in the census of 743: the true count was 6,202 households within the walls.

parts.before: The city walls were patched along 148 yards of their length near the Drovers' Gate.
parts.text: The founders' chest buried beneath the Founders' Arch was opened before the whole council and found to hold 879 silver coins.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, Leopold Jarnwell, a bookbinder from Highmarket, was remembered long afterwards for writing a satirical song about the council.

decoys.before: A travelling company of players performed on Flint Way, and one of their comedies was promptly banned by the aldermen.
decoys.text: A second chest, dug up under the Old Weighhouse, held 897 copper coins and a broken key.

parts.before: It is also recorded that the Tide Festival was kept with unusual splendour, and 274 paper lanterns were floated down the river.
parts.text: The races at the Apple Wake were won that year by a grey mare called Duchess of Mists.
parts.after: The price of dyed cloth rose to 11 silver marks a sack, and the people of Mudwharf grumbled about it in every tavern.

decoys.before: A scholar named Wenna Iverwell began a catalogue of the city's books, which was still unfinished forty years later.
decoys.text: A chestnut colt named Quicksilver Jenny came second in the races at the Apple Wake, to the fury of his owner.
decoys.after: Yannick Dunnwick left a bequest of 380 gold crowns to the almshouse on Copper Row.

parts.before: Wilmot Halley was appointed keeper of the city granary and held the post for 17 years.
parts.text: That year the watchword of the Night Watch was "quicksilver", and anyone abroad after curfew had to give it.
parts.after: Merchants from the Amber Coast brought news of war in the south, and prices rose accordingly.

decoys.before: Wolves were seen on the hills above Marrowby, and the shepherds kept watch in pairs.
decoys.text: The Day Watch, never to be outdone, chose the word "juniper".
decoys.after: Meanwhile, the market in Rookhill moved from Brine Way to the square in front of St. Bertram's.

parts.before: A fire broke out in a bookbinder's workshop on Anchor Way, but it was put out before it could spread to the Glass Steps.
parts.text: In those years the Tanners' Guild was led by Lisbet Sorrwick.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, Jorund Veyford, a lamplighter from Rookhill, was remembered long afterwards for writing a satirical song about the council.

parts.text: Lisbet Sorrwick died of a fever in the year 776 and was buried at St. Wendreda's.
parts.after: The chronicler notes, with some disapproval, that the Tanners' Guild spent 466 copper pennies on a single banquet that year.

decoys.before: The council met 7 times that year, mostly to argue about the drains of the Tanners' Quarter.
decoys.text: Lisbet Zorrwick, a wealthy wine merchant, died in the year 784.

parts.before: The harvest in the valley was poor, and bread was rationed in Lowbridge until the spring.
parts.text: The famous Widow's Stew of Fishergate called for exactly 15 threads of saffron, no more and no fewer.
parts.after: The toll-keepers of the Old Bridge went on strike, and for a week nobody could cross without paying twice.

decoys.before: It is also recorded that the Fishwives' Guild quarrelled with the Glassblowers' Guild over the use of the old weighhouse, and the matter went before the magistrates.
decoys.text: Salt-Crust Bream, its humbler cousin, used 35 cloves instead.
decoys.after: Meanwhile, a scholar named Wilmot Halley began a catalogue of the city's books, which was still unfinished forty years later.

parts.before: A fire broke out in a stonemason's workshop on Tallow Way, but it was put out before it could spread to the Old Harbour.
parts.text: On her last voyage the Crooked Pilgrim was commanded by Captain Soren Corby.
parts.after: It was, by all accounts, a quiet summer in Saltings.

parts.before: Later that year, a travelling company of players performed on Tallow Way, and one of their comedies was promptly banned by the aldermen.
parts.text: Soren Corby had been born in the hill village of Fernhollow, far from any sea.
parts.after: Rain fell for 4 days without stopping, and the lower streets of the Tanners' Quarter stood knee-deep in water.

decoys.before: Elowen Haldal and Greta Narkdal were seen arguing on Rope Walk about the price of herring, to the delight of the passers-by.
decoys.text: Captain Soren Korby was born in Wrenfold and never once lost a ship.
decoys.after: Nothing of great note happened in the Old Harbour that summer, except that a bear escaped from the menagerie and was found asleep in the Temple of the Lamp.

parts.before: The market in the Upper Terraces moved from Tallow Way to the square in front of the Temple of the Lamp.
parts.text: The Lightning Oak in the Old Green, the oldest tree in the city, was measured at 37 feet around the trunk.
parts.after: Pilgrims came to St. Ilse's in great numbers, many of them from the hill villages around Pellow Cross.

decoys.text: The Crooked Elm, which stood not far away, measured 33 feet around.
decoys.after: Cressen Garmore left a bequest of 367 copper pennies to the almshouse on Rope Walk.

parts.before: The coopers of Rookhill complained that the new regulations of the Apothecaries' Guild were written only to ruin them.
parts.text: The treaty of friendship with Karane was signed on the 12th day of April, in the hall of the Ropemakers' Guild.
parts.after: Rain fell for 22 days without stopping, and the lower streets of the Tanners' Quarter stood knee-deep in water.

decoys.before: The toll-keepers of the Cooper's Bridge went on strike, and for a week nobody could cross without paying twice.

source.text:
On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. But the samples Cordelia carried home in her rucksack made her famous, the crystal cave was named after the village of Sennick, and the climbers always insisted that the real hero of the journey had been a goat called Mabel.

source.text:
On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

Their base camp stood beside a frozen lake that the villagers called the Black Tarn. The expedition's doctor, Benedek Krauss, carried a medicine chest and a fiddle, which he played badly every night. The oldest climber was Brenna Brodsky, who was 59 years old and had climbed with the leader's father. The supplies had been carried up from the valley by 16 mules.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. But the samples Cordelia carried home in her rucksack made her famous, the crystal cave was named after the village of Sennick, and the climbers always insisted that the real hero of the journey had been a goat called Mabel.

parts.before: In the winter of 721, the Chandlers' Guild petitioned the council for the right to hold a market in the Narrows.
parts.text: The shipwrights bought 56 barrels of pitch brought from the forest of Blackwold.
parts.after: A dispute over a stolen weathervane between two families of the Narrows occupied the magistrates for 2 weeks.

parts.before: Pilgrims came to the Chapel of the Tides in great numbers, many of them from the hill villages around Marrowby.
parts.text: Charcoal-burners from the forest of Blackwold delivered 68 more barrels of pitch before the rains.
parts.after: The Jarnwell family of Highmarket sent their youngest son to be apprenticed to a glassblower in Saltings.

parts.before: Around this time, the council met 31 times that year, mostly to argue about the drains of Saltings.
parts.text: A last load of 19 barrels of pitch came from the forest of Blackwold in the autumn.
parts.after: Ships from Carrowmouth crowded the harbour; the Restless Gull alone carried 42 bales of wine.

decoys.before: The year 704 opened with rumours of war beyond the mountains.
decoys.text: The forest of Blackwood supplied 79 barrels of pitch, but the shipwrights judged it poor.
decoys.after: Perrin Carrgrave and Anselm Corford were seen arguing on Sparrow Yard about the price of timber, to the delight of the passers-by.

parts.before: The market in Rookhill moved from Sparrow Yard to the square in front of the Temple of the Lamp.
parts.text: The census of 743 counted 5,372 households within the walls.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, many of the older houses on Brine Way were rebuilt in brick after the long storm.

parts.before: According to the guild rolls, many of the older houses on Rope Walk were rebuilt in brick after the great fire.
parts.text: Clerks later found an error in the census of 743: the true count was 6,202 households within the walls.

parts.before: The city walls were patched along 148 yards of their length near the Drovers' Gate.
parts.text: The founders' chest buried beneath the Founders' Arch was opened before the whole council and found to hold 879 silver coins.
parts.after: According to the guild rolls, Leopold Jarnwell, a bookbinder from Highmarket, was remembered long afterwards for writing a satirical song about the council.

decoys.before: A travelling company of players performed on Flint Way, and one of their comedies was promptly banned by the aldermen.
decoys.text: A second chest, dug up under the Old Weighhouse, held 897 copper coins and a broken key.

parts.before: It is also recorded that the Tide Festival was kept with unusual splendour, and 274 paper lanterns were floated down the river.
parts.text: The races at the Apple Wake were won that year by a grey mare called Duchess of Mists.
parts.after: The price of dyed cloth rose to 11 silver marks a sack, and the people of Mudwharf grumbled about it in every tavern.

decoys.before: A scholar named Wenna Iverwell began a catalogue of the city's books, which was still unfinished forty years later.
decoys.text: A chestnut colt named Quicksilver Jenny came second in the races at the Apple Wake, to the fury of his owner.
decoys.after: Yannick Dunnwick left a bequest of 380 gold crowns to the almshouse on Copper Row.

parts.before: Wilmot Halley was appointed keeper of the city granary and held the post for 17 years.
parts.text: That year the watchword of the Night Watch was "quicksilver", and anyone abroad after curfew had to give it.
parts.after: Merchants from the Amber Coast brought news of war in the south, and prices rose accordingly.

decoys.before: Wolves were seen on the hills above Marrowby, and the shepherds kept watch in pairs.

source.text:
On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. But the samples Cordelia carried home in her rucksack made her famous, the crystal cave was named after the village of Sennick, and the climbers always insisted that the real hero of the journey had been a goat called Mabel.

source.text:
On 19 January 1933, an expedition of 14 climbers set out from the village of Sennick to attempt the unclimbed north face of Mount Vashti. Their leader was Cordelia Fairweather, a geologist who had spent most of her life studying the mountain from below and who was determined, at last, to see it from above.

The team's guide was Tobiah Ashgrove, who had grown up in Sennick and knew every path on the lower slopes. For luck, the climbers brought a goat named Mabel, which carried the heaviest packs without complaint and seemed to enjoy the climb more than anyone. Cordelia carried a brass telescope engraved with the names of her grandparents, and each evening she used it to study the ridges ahead.

They climbed slowly, roped together in pairs, cutting steps into the ice wherever the old snow had hardened. At night they huddled around a small stove and argued cheerfully about the route, the weather and whose turn it was to fetch water. The guide taught them songs from the valley, and the leader taught them the names of the rocks beneath their boots, which most of them had forgotten by morning.

Their base camp stood beside a frozen lake that the villagers called the Black Tarn. The expedition's doctor, Benedek Krauss, carried a medicine chest and a fiddle, which he played badly every night. The oldest climber was Brenna Brodsky, who was 59 years old and had climbed with the leader's father. The supplies had been carried up from the valley by 16 mules.

For the first week the weather was kind. They made steady progress and set up their highest camp at 4,457 metres, on a narrow shelf of rock below the summit ridge. Then the wind changed. A storm settled over the mountain and refused to move, and the climbers were trapped in their tents for 12 days, unable to climb higher or to retreat.

Their food ran low. By the end they were living on nothing but prunes and melted snow, rationed out by Tobiah one handful at a time. Mabel the goat, sheltering behind the largest tent, seemed the least troubled of them all. Every morning the climbers looked up at the ridge, and every morning the cloud sat on it like a lid. Nobody complained, but nobody laughed very much either.

When the storm finally lifted, Fairweather made a decision that surprised everyone: rather than push for the summit, they would go down while they still could. On the way down they found that a rockfall had opened a cave that had not been there before. Inside, the walls glittered with blue crystals that Cordelia recognised at once as something no geologist had ever described.

The expedition never reached the summit, and for years afterwards its critics called it a failure. But the samples Cordelia carried home in her rucksack made her famous, the crystal cave was named after the village of Sennick, and the climbers always insisted that the real hero of the journey had been a goat called Mabel.

const c=document.getElementById('c'),x=c.getContext('2d');let W,H;function fit(){W=c.width=innerWidth;H=c.height=innerHeight}fit();addEventListener('resize',fit);
let s={y:H/2,v:0,heat:40,score:0,best:0,pipes:[],t:0,state:'start',parts:[]};
function flap(){if(s.state!=='play'){s={...s,y:H/2,v:0,heat:40,score:0,pipes:[],state:'play'};return}s.v=-7;s.heat=Math.max(0,s.heat-6)}
addEventListener('keydown',e=>{if(e.code==='Space'||e.code==='ArrowUp'){e.preventDefault();flap()}});addEventListener('pointerdown',flap);
let last=performance.now();function loop(now){const dt=Math.min(40,now-last)/16.7;last=now;s.t+=dt;
if(s.state==='play'){s.v+=0.38*dt;s.y+=s.v*dt;s.heat=Math.min(100,s.heat+0.12*dt);if(s.t%90<dt)s.pipes.push({x:W,gap:120+Math.random()*(H-300),p:false});
for(const p of s.pipes){p.x-=3.2*dt;if(!p.p&&p.x<W*0.3){p.p=true;s.score++}if(p.x<W*0.3+18&&p.x+70>W*0.3-18&&(s.y<p.gap||s.y>p.gap+170))s.state='over'}
s.pipes=s.pipes.filter(p=>p.x>-80);if(s.y>H||s.y<0||s.heat>=100)s.state='over';s.best=Math.max(s.best,s.score)}
for(let i=0;i<3;i++)s.parts.push({x:W*0.3-14,y:s.y+Math.random()*10-5,vx:-2-Math.random()*2,vy:Math.random()*2-1,l:1});
const g=x.createLinearGradient(0,0,0,H);g.addColorStop(0,'#1a0f2e');g.addColorStop(1,'#3b1d1d');x.fillStyle=g;x.fillRect(0,0,W,H);
x.fillStyle='#4a5568';for(const p of s.pipes){x.fillRect(p.x,0,70,p.gap);x.fillRect(p.x,p.gap+170,70,H)}
for(const p of s.parts){p.x+=p.vx*dt;p.y+=p.vy*dt;p.l-=0.03*dt;x.fillStyle='rgba(255,'+Math.round(120+p.l*100)+',40,'+Math.max(0,p.l)+')';x.beginPath();x.arc(p.x,p.y,6*p.l+1,0,7);x.fill()}s.parts=s.parts.filter(p=>p.l>0);
x.fillStyle='#ffb347';x.beginPath();x.arc(W*0.3,s.y,16,0,7);x.fill();x.fillStyle='#fff';x.beginPath();x.arc(W*0.3+6,s.y-5,4,0,7);x.fill();
x.fillStyle='#222';x.fillRect(20,20,220,18);x.fillStyle=s.heat>75?'#ff4d4d':'#ffa726';x.fillRect(20,20,2.2*s.heat,18);x.fillStyle='#fff';x.font='bold 14px system-ui';x.fillText('HEAT',250,34);
x.font='bold 36px system-ui';x.textAlign='center';x.fillText(s.score,W/2,70);x.font='16px system-ui';x.fillText('best '+s.best,W/2,95);
if(s.state!=='play'){x.font='bold 42px system-ui';x.fillText(s.state==='start'?'EMBER WING':'GAME OVER',W/2,H/2-20);x.font='20px system-ui';x.fillText('Space / click to '+(s.state==='start'?'start':'restart'),W/2,H/2+20)}x.textAlign='left';
requestAnimationFrame(loop)}requestAnimationFrame(loop);</script></body></html>

x.fillStyle='#111';x.fillRect(20,H-40,200,16);x.fillStyle='#ff7043';x.fillRect(20,H-40,2*power,16);
x.fillStyle='#fff';x.font='bold 28px system-ui';x.fillText('Goals '+score+' / '+shots+'   best '+best,20,40);x.font='18px system-ui';x.fillText(msg,20,70);
